Q: LPCSTR, LPCTSTR and LPTSTR A:

8-bit AnsiStrings

  • char: 8-bit character (underlying C/C++ data type)
  • CHAR: alias of char (Windows data type)
  • LPSTR: null-terminated string of CHAR (Long Pointer)
  • LPCSTR: constant null-terminated string of CHAR (Long Pointer Constant)

16-bit UnicodeStrings

  • wchar_t: 16-bit character (underlying C/C++ data type)
  • WCHAR: alias of wchar_t (Windows data type)
  • LPWSTR: null-terminated string of WCHAR (Long Pointer)
  • LPCWSTR: constant null-terminated string of WCHAR (Long Pointer Constant)

depending on UNICODE define

  • TCHAR: alias of WCHAR if UNICODE is defined; otherwise CHAR
  • LPTSTR: null-terminated string of TCHAR (Long Pointer)
  • LPCTSTR: constant null-terminated string of TCHAR (Long Pointer Constant)

So:

Item 8-bit (Ansi) 16-bit (Wide) Varies
character CHAR WCHAR TCHAR
string LPSTR LPWSTR LPTSTR
string (const) LPCSTR LPCWSTR LPCTSTR

Bonus Reading

TCHAR → Text Char

Why is the default 8-bit codepage called "ANSI"?

From Unicode and Windows XP
by Cathy Wissink
Program Manager, Windows Globalization
Microsoft Corporation
May 2002

Despite the underlying Unicode support on Windows NT 3.1, code page support continued to be necessary for many of the higher-level applications and components included in the system, explaining the pervasive use of the “A” [ANSI] versions of the Win32 APIs rather than the “W” [“wide” or Unicode] versions. (The term “ANSI” as used to signify Windows code pages is a historical reference, but is nowadays a misnomer that continues to persist in the Windows community. The source of this comes from the fact that the Windows code page 1252 was originally based on an ANSI draft, which became ISO Standard 8859-1. However, in adding code points to the range reserved for control codes in the ISO standard, the Windows code page 1252 and subsequent Windows code pages originally based on the ISO 8859-x series deviated from ISO. To this day, it is not uncommon to have the development community, both within and outside of Microsoft, confuse the 8859-1 code page with Windows 1252, as well as see “ANSI” or “A” used to signify Windows code page support.)

Q: I get stuck learning HTML, CSS, JAVASCRIPT (I AM A STUDENT) A:

You're not alone. Many students, junior devs, graduated, what not. All commonly struggle to put together concepts they've learned into something meaningful. Specially nowadays, the burdening curse of AI can get into anyone's way of that well feared Impostor syndrome. Copy-pasting from AI, YT, SO, etc. - the same.
You, instead, chose The way; to (re-) write it on your own, from first-to-last character, until it sits or fits. With this mindset alone, believe me - you're already in the fewer enviable minority.
Effective? Put it this way: "Repetitio est mater studiorum". And I kid you not. We've all spent endless time repeating the hardest parts of HTML (syntax, SEO, close, or not-to-close), CSS (oh boy... gridding, positioning, cross-browser, quirks, specificity, animations, whatnot), JS (functions, patterns, prototypes, classes, modules, libraries, frameworks, ecosystems... you name it) and to be frank it has never ended since. Not to the most of us. And not to mention that we all had to learn other languages and tools to incorporate those beautifully crafted UIs with a backend, databases, OS, etc. In the end, it's all knowledge gained by constantly and consistently writing and re-writing code, repeating the same patterns all over again - or learning new ones, one click away from the respective documentation. With interest and understanding, willing to build something, better, useful, new. As others have mentioned, find something that drives your curiosity and makes you happy. To end with, why are hackers commonly regarded as the brightest engineers? Because they think outside of the box, find intricate ingenious yet simple ways of break-it or make-it! That curiosity and passion is what we all strive to. Not being afraid to fail along the way (might be just a ;...). Find it in yourself. One character at a time.

Q: Comparing a character using the || or operator always returning true A:

Your code returns true if woord.charAt(i) is 'a', otherwise it returns the string 'e'. Since both true and 'e' are truthy, they are both considered to be true when encountered in a Boolean context (which per your question I imagine you are doing).

Explanation

Since == has a higher operator precedence than ||, your code is equivalent to (woord.charAt(i) == 'a') || ('e' || 'i' || 'o' || 'u').

The || operator returns its leftmost truthy operand, or false if neither is truthy.

woord.charAt(i) == 'a' is truthy value of true when charAt returns the string 'a', and the falsey value of false otherwise. The value of 'e' || 'i' || 'o' || 'u' is 'e', since 'e' is truthy.

The expression (woord.charAt(i) == 'a') || ('e' || 'i' || 'o' || 'u') therefore returns true when charAt returns 'a', and 'e' when it doesn't. Both of these possible values are truthy, so the overall expression is truthy.

Q: How to share websocket context in quart A:

quart.websocket is a LocalProxy() object that resolves to a WebSocket() object when in websocket context. If you want to use the websocket outside of the handler then store the real websocket object instead of the LocalProxy() by calling quart.websocket._get_current_object().

To clarify:

websockets=[]

@app.websocket("/ws")
async def ws():
    websockets.append(quart.websocket) # This would store LocalProxy()
    websockets.append(quart.websocket._get_current_object()) # This would store Websocket()

Then somewhere else:

websockets[0].send(...) # Websocket context not required

Q: Is it possible to see dateTime for file history in GitKraken? A:

There is a little gear in the right top corner of the graph section.

There you can find the option to show a "Date / Time" column with the absolute timestamp of every commit.

You can further customize the datetime format in the Settings -> UI Customization section.
